title: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
hookLine: a blacksmith who suffered for his faith in Mecca, and lived to see the community grow

cards: I won't pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad. A man in Mecca says that to the craftsman he owes. The craftsman is a blacksmith named Khabbab, come to collect for work already done.
The man who owes him is al-As ibn Wa'il. The bill is real: the work is done, and the money is owed. The price he puts on paying it is Khabbab's faith.
Today: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, the blacksmith.

teach.h: NOT UNTIL YOU DIE AND RISE AGAIN.
teach.b: That scene is Khabbab's own telling, in Sahih al-Bukhari. He answered al-As that he would not disbelieve, not until al-As died and was raised again. Bukhari connects verses in surah nineteen to that exchange.
Tradition says Khabbab paid for his faith with his body too, that he was made to lie on hot coals, and that years later he showed the scars on his back. The texts keep something quieter as well.
In another report in Bukhari, Khabbab remembers going to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who was resting on his cloak in the shade of the Kaaba.

teach.h: WON'T YOU ASK GOD TO HELP US?
teach.b: Won't you ask God to help us? The Prophet sat up. He spoke of believers before them who had suffered terribly and still not turned from their faith.

teach.h: A RIDER WHO FEARS NO ONE BUT GOD.
teach.b: Then he said God would complete this matter, until a rider could travel from San'a to Hadramawt fearing no one but God, and the wolf for his sheep. But you are in a hurry, he said.
That's a hard answer to hear when you are the one hurting. It doesn't deny the pain. It widens the frame.
And Khabbab lived to see the frame widen. A third report in Bukhari has him, much later, remembering the companions who emigrated.
Some died before tasting any reward, he says, and he names Mus'ab ibn Umayr, whom we have met on this road.
And some of us, Khabbab says, have seen our fruit ripen, and we are picking it.
In his own reports, what he holds on to is not that the fire was small, but the wider frame the Prophet showed him.

how: Muslims tell Khabbab's story from his own reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, where he speaks of his trade, of asking the Prophet for help in Mecca, and of the companions who did and did not live to see the community grow.

o: the blacksmith who kept his faith over an unpaid bill
the merchant who refused to pay a Muslim craftsman
a smith who forged swords for the army at Badr

games.q: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt — tap the pairs.
p: where he asked the Prophet for help

s: al-As refused to pay Khabbab unless he gave up his faith
Khabbab tells it in Bukhari: I won't pay until you disbelieve in Muhammad.
the Prophet told Khabbab his suffering didn't matter
he spoke of believers before them who endured, and of a coming safety, and said: you are in a hurry.
Khabbab died before the community grew
he lived to say: some of us have seen our fruit ripen, and we are picking it.

games.q: you are Khabbab. a man who owes you money says he'll pay only if you give up your faith. what do you say?
o: give in, just this once, to get paid.
refuse: not until you die and are raised again.
drop the debt and walk away silent.
games.why: Bukhari keeps his answer: he would not disbelieve, not until al-As died and was raised again. verses in surah nineteen are linked to the exchange.

practice: This week ran from Rufaydah's tent, through al-Shifa, Umm Sulaym, Hassan, Ka'b and Suhayb, to Khabbab.

Sit up a little straighter than is easy, and stay there; it isn't suffering, just a small chosen effort, and you can let it stand for someone you're helping or something you're building. If you pray, you can ask God for patience.

wordCard.voice: Khabbab. The blacksmith of Mecca who would not give up his faith for an unpaid debt, and lived to see the fruit ripen. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Khabbab, son of al-Aratt, the blacksmith.

carryVoice: Your line: the blacksmith endured. He lived to see the fruit ripen. That's day eight hundred fifty-four.
